prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought the accuracy and stability of atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first and the lattice clock second, and having read all eight ballots I now put the lattice clock first. Four members place it in their top three (Kroll and Lindroth first, Mehlig and I second), and no one has a substantive scientific objection to it. It combines a clean originating idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which removes the trade-off between atom number and motional shifts) with an experimental programme (Ye's strontium clocks, cavity-stabilised lasers, many-body and spin-squeezing extensions) that took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. The result has been confirmed independently in several national and university laboratories, it is already used for relativistic geodesy and for tests of fundamental constants, and it underpins the discussion about redefining the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: two named people, one conceptual and one experimental, with a clear link between them. Maturity is high and the timing is natural.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the share of credit at the margins. Lemonde, Gill, and other strontium and ytterbium groups reached comparable performance, so the Ye slot is partly a judgement about who drove the field. There is also a scope question after 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (ion clocks and single quantum systems). The committee has to show that the lattice clock is a distinct step and not an incremental extension of those prizes. The claim is solid but not a discovery of new phenomena. It is a measurement capability whose most striking consequences, such as a redefined second or geodetic and dark-matter searches, are still mostly prospective.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first, judging the physics from her atomic-physics expertise: original idea, 1e-18 performance, and broad independent confirmation, with the Katori-versus-Ye credit division the main doubt.
responses.response: I agree and I give her atomic-physics judgement more weight than my own, since I am not an atomic physicist. I would answer the credit worry by noting that the two names have different roles, concept and proof of accuracy, so the pairing follows the actual structure of the achievement. I would still ask her whether she thinks Ye's role is better described as the accuracy and many-body programme or as a distinct invention, because that determines how the citation should be worded. I would write the citation around the lattice clock and its accuracy, and not around spectroscopy in general, to avoid reopening the combs and ion clocks.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks black-hole shadow imaging (B054) first because it makes strong-field gravity directly observable, while admitting that credit in a roughly 300-person collaboration is hard to allocate to three people.
responses.response: I take the science seriously: the 2019 and 2022 images are real discoveries in my own broad area of observation. But I disagree with ranking it first. His own caveat is the decisive one, since the Falcke, Doeleman and Zensus split depends on contested conventions about who led a very large collaboration, and the tests of general relativity are limited by astrophysical modelling. That makes it a weaker prize candidate than a clearly attributed invention. I would keep it in view for a later year, and I do not see it as a rival to the lattice clock this year.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B022) first and the lattice clock second, noting that the phenomenology has been reproduced widely though the pairing mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: We agree on the top two and differ only in order, and I find his case for B022 serious. The theory-plus-experiment triple is clean and the field is large. My reservation is timing and attribution on the experimental side. The discovery is about eight years old, the superconductivity mechanism is open, and other experimental groups contributed. The lattice clock has a longer record of independent confirmation across continents, so I would put it ahead. If the committee prefers B022 I would not oppose it, and I would keep it as my first alternative if the clock fails.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first, with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (B037) second, and notes that Ye's group brought the clock to record accuracy while Katori made the original proposal.
responses.response: I agree on the clock and I accept his point that the independent confirmation is strong. I am less convinced by pairing it with B037 in a shared prize. The two share optical lattices but are distinct achievements, a metrology instrument and a quantum simulator, and B037 would need up to four names, which breaks the three-person limit. I would treat B037 as a separate case for a future year and avoid a combined citation that dilutes the clock.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B016) first and notes the possible overlap with the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits and macroscopic quantum effects, and the difficulty of choosing three of Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff.
responses.response: I think his own overlap point is the main difficulty, and so is the four-name problem. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits very recently, and a cQED prize this soon would need a clear scope statement. It is an important candidate and I accept the argument that it is the architecture behind most superconducting processors, but I would not prefer it in the current year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct advance from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, or sees it as an extension of those.
The credit of Lemonde, Gill and other strontium and ytterbium groups relative to Ye, which I cannot settle from the supplied record.
Whether IceCube (B007) should rank above the clock if the committee values opening a new observational window over a measurement capability.
Whether the allocation within B007 between Halzen, Spiering and the Baikal and DUMAND pioneers could be settled.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B025, B022 or the other non-astroparticle candidates. I have professional ties to the astroparticle community through PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur, and my KTH group works with detectors of a related kind, so I discount my opening enthusiasm for B007 (IceCube) and would consider recusal or a discounted view if it were the leading candidate.
